profile.summary: Jeremiah arises at a time when Judah still seemed relatively stable, but this security was illusory. The prophet is called by God to announce judgment on a people who had strayed from the Lord through idolatry and the unfaithfulness of the covenant. His ministry goes through the ascension of Babylon, the end of the brief revival under Josiah, the persistent refusal of kings, priests and prophets in hearing the divine word, the fall of Jerusalem and exile. The book records not only the message of judgment, but also the inner struggle of the prophet himself, who suffers in proclaiming destruction over his people. At the same time, Jeremiah preserves a note of hope: God calls repentance, promises to restore a remnant and announces a future renewed relationship with his people, culminating in the promise of restoration and a righteous ruler.
profile.setting: The historical scene is the end of the kingdom of Judah, between the decline of Assyria and the ascension of Babylon. Before the birth of Jeremiah, Manasseh took Judah to a period of strong idolatry; his son Ammon followed the same course. Josiah, as a boy when he became king, promoted an important religious reform, with the destruction of idols and the reparation of the temple, especially after the rediscovering of the Book of Law. This revival, however, was brief: the death of Josiah in 609 BC marked the beginning of the national collapse. After that, Judah was among international pressures and internal crises, with kings such as Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah oscillating between resistance, submission and disobedience. Babylon, especially under Nebuchadnezzar II, dominated the region, besieged Jerusalem, broke its walls in 586 BC, destroyed the temple and took many into exile. As for the composition of the book, the introduction suggests that part of the material came from messages dictated to Baruch and then expanded, but also states that the book was being gathered over time; therefore, the date and final form present some degree of editorial development.

structure.label: Called by Jeremiah
structure.description: God chooses and commissions Jeremiah as his messenger.

structure.label: Confrontation with Judah
structure.description: God denounces idolatry, proclaims invasion and judgment, and Jeremiah proceeds to understand the divine purposes more deeply.

structure.label: Conflicts with leaders and prophets
structure.description: Jeremiah enters into verbal clashes with kings, priests and other prophets, exposing the corruption of the leaderships.

structure.label: Hope of restoration
structure.description: The promise of restoration, a new covenant relationship and a righteous descendant emerges and a just descendant who will bring salvation.

structure.label: Fall of Jerusalem and its unfoldings
structure.description: The siege, the destruction of the temple and the city, and the events after the fall, including the refusal of the people to remain on earth, are in the midst of the deception.

structure.label: Judgments against the nations
structure.description: Oracles announce the judgment of neighboring peoples for their idolatry and cruelty, while reaffirming the hope of deliverance and restoration for Israel.

structure.label: Final historical Appendix
structure.description: Report of the last days of Jerusalem, resuming and confirming the memory of the fall of the city.

themes: Exclusive fidelity to the Lord against idolatry
Divine judgment as a response to the breaking of the covenant
The inner suffering of the prophet before his mission
The Responsibility of Spiritual and Political Leadership
Hope of restoration, remnant and new alliance
readingKeys: Notice how Jeremiah alternates accusations, judicial discourses, and autobiographical narratives; this helps to realize when the text is arguing, lamenting or reporting events.
Note the recurring contrast between the false security of Judah and the reality of judgment: political covenants, temple and rites do not replace repentance and obedience.
Read carefully the passages of hope, especially in chapters 3033, as a divine response to catastrophe, and not as her denial; restoration comes after judgment.
profile.cautions: The introduction presented highlights that Jeremiah brings together materials from different moments and possibly from different textual collections; therefore, the exact date and the final process of composition are not totally right. There are also two old textual traditions with relevant differences in extension and organization. When reading, it is advisable to avoid treating all the statements as if they were on the same narrative or chronological level, because the book combines oracles, historical narratives and prophetic autobiography. Moreover, the promises of restoration do not nullify the gravity of the judgment; they appear as grace granted to a people disciplined by their infidelity.

dossier.narratedEra: The book is set above all in the late 7th century BC and in the first decades of the 6th century BC, since the call of Jeremiah in the 13th year of Josiah (627 BC, according to the introduction of Tyndale) until the days after the fall of Jerusalem, including the deportation and the period in which the prophet still records events in the midst of the remaining survivors. The narrative follows the decline of Judah under Assyrian, Egyptian and, above all Babylonian pressure, culminating in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
dossier.compositionEra: Tyndale's notes suggest that Jeremiah dictated messages to Baruch in the 4th year of Jehoiakim (605 BC), forming a first roll that was destroyed and remade, with later additions; the work would have been essentially completed around 580 BC. Matthew Henry also notes that the book's materials are not necessarily in strict chronological order. The notes also mention two ancient textual traditions - Hebrew and Greek - with the Septuagint produced around 250 BC and about 2,700 shorter words. This matters because the reader must distinguish the time portrayed from the editorial formation of the book.

politics.title: Judah between Assyrian domination and the decline of the kingdom
politics.detail: Before the birth of Jeremiah, Assyria dominated the ancient Near East; Manasseh became a vassal of Assyria and was associated with idolatrous worship. Amon followed the same way until he was murdered, and then Josiah was crowned as a child.
politics.readingImpact: The beginning of the book does not speak of a sudden crisis, but of a already spiritually corroded realm. Jeremiah's denunciation gains weight for appearing in a context of prolonged political and religious decay.

politics.title: Josias Reforms and brief renovation window
politics.detail: Josiah rejected idolatry, promoted destruction of altars and repairs in the temple, and in the restoration the discovery of the Book of the Law laid the preaching of Jeremiah.
politics.readingImpact: Jeremiah does not appear as a mere prophet of disgrace: his message is born in a real window of reformation, but the reading shows that this renewal was fragile and did not prevent further judgment.

politics.title: Rise of Nebuchadnezzar and subdued Judah
politics.detail: Between 612 and 605 BC, the Babylonians defeated Assyrians and Egyptians; then between 605 and 586 B.C., Nebuchadnezzar attacked, subdued and finally destroyed Judah and Jerusalem.
politics.readingImpact: The book should be read as prophecy amid real imperial change. The threat of the north is not generic: it is linked to the Babylonian expansion that has redefined regional policy.

politics.title: Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah as vassal kings and tenses
politics.detail: Jehoiakim trusted in Egypt against Babylon and violently opposed Jeremiah; Jeconiah reigned only three months; Zedekiah reigned as a vassal of Babylon, was weak and undecided, and ended up breaking his commitment to the Babylonian king.
politics.readingImpact: Jeremiah's resistance to political alliances appears as fidelity to the covenant with the Lord, not as simply opposition to the government. The kings of Judah are presented as incapable of sustaining national survival by diplomatic means.
politics.reference: Introduction Tyndale, "Setting" and "Summary"; cap. 52 in Tyndale.

politics.title: Siege, breach and collapse of Jerusalem
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction places the siege in January 588 BC, the breach of the walls in July 586 BC, the destruction of the temple and the exile of many residents; Jeremiah 52 reinforces the final fall and deportation.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Jeremiah 34-45 and 52 is shaped by this sequence of ruin: the prophet's warnings are confirmed in concrete historical events, emphasizing his prophetic integrity.

customs.title: Annual festivals in the temple and the public square of worship
customs.detail: Jeremiah 26:2 notes that the people gathered in the temple hall during the annual feasts; also stands out the use of sacred space as a place of debate and accusation.
customs.readingImpact: The temple was not only a place of devotion, but also a public assembly. This helps to understand why Jeremiah's words provoked so much hostility and why his preaching reached the centre of community life.

customs.title: Processes at the gate of the city
customs.detail: The notes explain that courts were held at the gate of the city, covered space and with several chambers, where elders assessed conflicts and commercial life circulated.
customs.readingImpact: Jeremiah's judgment is not an isolated detail: it reflects the legal custom of the time and shows how the prophecy was debated in public institutions, not just in the religious sphere.

customs.title: Ideolatric cult, parties and "sexual freedom," as a competitor appeal
customs.detail: Tyndale describes the fascination of pagan rituals, feasts, and sexual freedom as part of the attraction of idolatry in Judah.
customs.readingImpact: This explains why Jeremiah's denunciation was not only theological; she confronted socially seductive pleasures and practices rooted in daily life, making the call to repentance more costly.

customs.title: Urban life under siege and loss of goods
customs.detail: The introduction associates war with the loss of city, temple, family, wealth, and freedom; it also mentions that exile and escape to Egypt have reached the rest of the population.
customs.readingImpact: The book must be read with awareness of the material impact of judgment. It is not just about religious language, but about rupture of housing, security and community continuity.

customs.title: The remnant poor after the fall
customs.detail: Jeremiah 52:15 mentions - some of the poorest of the people, and the note notes that the formulation was added; the chapter also emphasizes the group left on earth after destruction.
customs.readingImpact: The narrative does not end with the deported elite; there is a remaining and impoverished community. This directs reading to precarious survival, not just for the monumental event of the fall.

language.title: The "Messman" system and the royal voice of Jeremiah
language.detail: The introduction describes the ancient diplomatic pattern in which a messenger led the authority of the sovereign; in 1:1-19, Jeremiah is presented as one who speaks to the authority of the divine king.
language.readingImpact: Prophetic language is not merely private or devotional. The reader understands Jeremiah as an official ambassador, which intensifies the responsibility of hearing or rejecting his word.
language.reference: Introduction Tyndale, "Literary Features: The Messenger System"; Jer 1:1-19.

language.title: Judicial structure and vocabulary of court
language.detail: Tyndale points out that Jeremiah uses forensic language: the Lord acts as the author of the action, judge and executor; 2:9 is cited as the opening of a cause against Judah.
language.readingImpact: This legal framework changes the reading of many warnings: they are not loose emotional explosions, but formal accusations of broken alliance.

language.title: The pun on the branch of almond tree and the watchman of God
language.detail: In 1:11-12, the note explains the sound game between the word for almond tree and the word for "vigiar," relating the first flowering of the tree to divine vigilance.
language.readingImpact: The image communicates speed and surveillance. The reader realizes that the judgment announced is not distant or uncertain: God is attentive and acts at the right time.

language.title: Invasion of the north, though Babylon is on the east
language.detail: The note of 1:13-14 explains that although Babylon was to the east, the desert forced the armies to attack Judah from the north; the image is of boiling water and military terror.
language.readingImpact: The geographical direction reinforces the prophecy and avoids simplistic literal reading. The image helps to understand why the "north" in Jeremiah is a recurring cause of threat.

language.title: Jeremiah as "prophet ram" and autobiographical narrator
language.detail: Matthew Henry calls him a weeping prophet and Tyndale highlights autobiographical narratives in which the prophet reveals his inner tension, especially between the divine order of speaking and his desire for peace.
language.readingImpact: The language of the book does not only convey external judgment; it allows to see the inner suffering of the prophet, which deepens the pastoral and spiritual reading of the text.
language.reference: Matthew Henry, introduction; Tyndale, "Literary Features: Narratives" and "Meaning and Message."

timeline.title: 627 BC: called Jeremiah in the reign of Josiah
timeline.detail: Tyndale places chapter 1 in 627 BC and the beginning of Jeremiah's ministry in the 13th year of Josiah; Matthew Henry also says that he began young in the 13th year of Josiah.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader begins the prophecy in a period still relatively stable, before the final collapse, which highlights the ignored urgency of the warnings.
timeline.reference: Jer 1; introductions by Tyndale and Matthew Henry.

timeline.title: 605 BC: roll dictated to Baruch
timeline.detail: In the 4th year of Jehoiakim Jeremiah sent messages to Baruch; the king destroyed the scroll, which was rewritten with an addition of much more material.
timeline.readingImpact: The formation of the book is linked to the real crisis and conflict. This helps to read the initial chapters as preserved messages amidst the official persecution.
timeline.reference: Introduction Tyndale, "Authorship and Date"; cf. Jer 36:1-32.

timeline.title: 597 BC: fall of Judah and the replacement of Jeconiah by Zedekiah
timeline.detail: Tyndale claims that in April 597 BC the Babylonians defeated Judah, took Jeconiah and placed Zedekiah as vassal.
timeline.readingImpact: The change of king is not mere dynastic detail; it marks a new stage of dependence, in which Jeremiah confronts the policy of survival of the kingdom.

timeline.title: 588-586 BC: siege and final destruction of Jerusalem
timeline.detail: The siege began in January 588 BC, and in July 586 BC the Babylonians broke the walls, destroyed the temple and devastated the city.
timeline.readingImpact: Chapters of judgment and crisis narratives should be read in the light of this historical outcome, which confirms the core of the prophetic proclamation.

timeline.title: Up to about 580 BC: essential completion of the book
timeline.detail: The introduction suggests that the book was essentially complete around 580 BC, including events until Jeremiah's departure from Egypt.
timeline.readingImpact: This guides the reading to a prolonged editorial process, in which later materials were aggregated without erasing the central testimony of the prophet.

investigation: The introduction of Tyndale affirms two textual traditions of Jeremiah, but the attached notes do not develop in detail the differences in content beyond size and rearrangement.
Matthew Henry mentions traditions about the end of Jeremiah in Egypt and apocryphal accounts, but the notes do not allow to confirm these episodes as historical.
The internal chronology of the book is presented as approximate, and there are chapters with material out of a strict temporal order; therefore, exact dates must be treated with caution.
The available notes are selective: they cover mainly 1, 26 and 52, in addition to the general introductions; customs and language of other chapters appear only indirectly.
Some statements about the composition are inferential in the notes (probable, "probably," not independent documentary certainties.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the attached notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry. Therefore, it privileges what they explicitly affirm and avoids complementary with external knowledge, even when something would be historically plausible. The coverage is unequal: there are many data on political context, so-called prophetic, temple court and chapter 52, but little direct information about economics, family, food or domestic life in the body of the provided notes. There is also a distinction between narrative setting and composition dating, but textual tradition and academic debates appear only briefly in the sources. Where notes infer dates, authorship or editorial additions, this was classified as interpretation and not as independent proof.
